newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl dismisses talk of EMU timetable change.
newsitem.headline: Kohl dismisses talk of EMU timetable change.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Wednesday dismissed speculation that changes could be made to the timetable for European monetary union that would launch the euro in 1999 but still allow countries to meet the criteria.
Asked by Pro7 television whether "the clock will be stopped", Kohl was quoted in a summary of the interview as saying: "No, not a bit."
"We will make the necessary decisions based on the criteria in the Maastricht treaty within the prescribed timetable and launch the euro," Kohl said.
"Anything else would have catastrophic consequences for the German economy, a catastrophic impact on the labour market, for our currency and others," he added.

Kohl was responding to a report in the Berliner Morgenpost newspaper, which said senior officials in his coalition were mulling a plan to delay the start of economic and monetary union by one year to 2000 and shorten the transition phase for the euro's introduction to two years from three.

The paper quoted an unidentified senior coalition source as saying the one year delay for the start of EMU could help Germany and other countries to qualify for the strict Maastricht Treaty fiscal requirements.
"It would be better if we could just freeze the euro clock for one year in 1999," a high-ranking coalition source was quoted as saying.
The report could not be confirmed.
The source added that the suggestion for such a delay would have to come from another European country and not from Germany.

Under the plan, the euro would be introduced as originally planned in 2002. But rather than having a three year transition period before that date, the euro candidates would shorten that to two years.
The economic data for 1998, rather than 1997, would be used to determine the nations qualifying.
The paper said the idea would also appeal to the French in part because the new Socialist government would welcome the idea of more time to prepare.

The sources were quoted as saying Chancellor Helmut Kohl would also not likely oppose the plan. It would also be easier for Germany if the decision on who qualifies for the euro would be made after the next general election due in September 1998.
